title: Man. Post. Cap. II §XVII: Garissoles on mediate theologians / Placeus — discrimen false; before §XIX
pass_a_gloss: GAR. I judge that was the mind of those Theologians who teach that Adam's sin is imputed to us mediately, or by the mediation of our corruption and viciousness. Aegidius Hunnius article on sin Question 7; Walaeus Defense of Molinaeus chapter 8. But truly far other is the sense of the Learned Men who use this distinction of prior and posterior imputation. Inasmuch as 1. they absolutely deny that which we called common, prior and immediate, and so on. 2. Because they explain the posterior and mediate or singular far otherwise, namely so that they claim it in no way looks to Adam's actual and personal sin itself, but ought to be referred only to our own original vice and native and hereditary corruption. PLAC. Both this difference is openly false. And first indeed: For Aegidius Hunnius and Walaeus denied immediate imputation so expressly that they could not have done so more expressly. He says Adam's fall is imputed to us his posterity not immediately and of itself, but mediately and on account of another. Likewise, that one offense yields to us unto condemnation only mediately. What does that negation mean, not immediately and of itself? What the exclusive, Only mediately? What is it to deny immediate imputation, if this is not? But this man denies the possibility of that imputation, and strengthens his negation by an argument drawn from God's justice. You have the place above at page 22, as the earlier at page 20. The second also is so openly false that I cannot wonder enough how the Learned man could obtain from himself to put it forth. For on the contrary I contend that mediate imputation looks to Adam's actual and personal sin itself; nor was it ever used by me of another sin, or, what is more, could it be used.
pass_b_english: Garissoles: I take that to have been the mind of those theologians who teach that Adam's sin is imputed to us mediately—through our corruption and viciousness as means (Aegidius Hunnius, article on sin, Question 7; Walaeus, Defense of Molinaeus, chapter 8). But the learned men who use this prior/posterior imputation distinction mean something quite different. (1) They absolutely deny what we called the common, prior, immediate imputation, and so on. (2) They explain the posterior, mediate, or singular far otherwise—claiming it in no way looks to Adam's actual personal sin, but must be referred only to our own original vice and native hereditary corruption. Placeus: Both differences are plainly false. First: Hunnius and Walaeus denied immediate imputation as expressly as speech allows. Hunnius says Adam's fall is imputed to us his posterity not immediately and of itself, but mediately and on account of something else—and that that one offense yields to condemnation only mediately. What does not immediately and of itself mean? What does the exclusive only mediately mean? If that is not denying immediate imputation, what is? As for this writer, he denies even the possibility of that imputation and props the denial with an argument from God's justice; see above, page 22 (and earlier, page 20). The second difference is so openly false I cannot wonder enough how the learned man brought himself to say it. On the contrary I maintain that mediate imputation looks to Adam's actual personal sin itself; I have never used it of another sin, nor—what is more—could it be so used.
source_text:
GAR. Eam existimo fuisse mentem illis Theologis, qui peccatum Adae docent nobis imputari mediate, sive mediante corruptione & vitiositate nostra. Aegid. Hunnius artic. de pecc. Quaest. 7. Walaeus Defens. Molin. cap. 8. Enimvero longe alius Doctis Viris sensus, qui hac prioris & posterioris imputationis distinctione utuntur. Quandoquidem 1. eam, quam diximus communem, priorem & immediatam, absolute negant &c. 2. Quia posteriorem & mediatam sive singularem longe aliter exponunt, ita scilicet ut eam pretendant nulla ratione ad ipsum actuale & personale Adami peccatum respicere, sed ad nostrum ipsorum duntaxat originale vitium nativamque & hereditariam corruptionem referri debere.

PLAC. Utrumque hoc discrimen aperte falsum est. Et primum quidem: Negarunt enim imputationem immediatam Aegidius Hunnius & Walaeus tam diserte, ut disertius non potuerint. Ille ait lapsum Adami non immediate & per se, sed mediate & propter aliud nobis ejus posteris imputari. Item, unum illud delictum nobis ad condemnationem cedere tantum mediate. Quid sibi vult illa negatio, non immediate & per se? Quid exclusiva, Tantum mediate? Quid est negare imputationem immediatam, si hoc non est? Hic vero imputationis illius possibilitatem negat, suamque negationem firmat ducto a Dei justitia argumento. Locum habes supra pag. 22. uti superiorem pag. 20. Secundum etiam tam aperte falsum est, ut satis mirari non possim, quomodo a se Vir Doctus impetrare potuerit, ut id proferret. Contra enim contendo imputationem mediatam ad ipsum actuale & personale Adami peccatum respicere; nec de alio peccato a me unquam usurpatam fuisse, aut, quod amplius est, usurpari potuisse.
